questions.question: What does a monoid add to the structure of a semigroup?
options: A determinant.
An identity element.
An inner product.
A requirement that every element has an inverse.

questions.question: Does a monoid require every element to have an inverse?
options: Yes, but only if the operation is addition.
Yes. Every monoid is automatically a group.
No. That extra condition leads toward groups.
No, because monoids cannot have identity elements.

questions.question: Why is every group automatically a monoid?
options: A group has an associative operation and an identity element.
A group has no binary operation
A group has no inverse elements.
A group operation is not closed, unlike the operation of a monoid

questions.question: What role does the identity element play in a monoid?
options: It swaps the order of multiplication.
It makes every product equal to zero.
It is a neutral element for the operation.
It replaces associativity.

questions.question: Why is $(\mathbb{N}_0,+)$ a monoid?
options: Addition is associative and $0$ is an identity element.
Addition is not closed on $\mathbb{N}_0$.
Every natural number has an additive inverse in $\mathbb{N}_0$.
The identity element is $1$.

questions.question: Why is $(\mathbb{N},+)$ a monoid?
options: Addition is associative and closed, and $0$ is an identity
Every natural number has an additive inverse in $\mathbb{N}$
$1$ is the identity because $n+1=n$
Addition is commutative, and commutativity alone defines a monoid

questions.question: For $n\times n$ matrices under multiplication, what is the monoid identity?
options: The matrix with all diagonal entries zero.
$I_n$
The zero matrix.
Any invertible matrix.

questions.question: Why is the set of all $n\times n$ matrices (for a fixed $n$) under multiplication a monoid but not a group?
options: Singular matrices do not have multiplicative inverses.
Matrix multiplication is not associative.
Matrix multiplication has no identity.
The product of square matrices is never square.

questions.question: If a monoid is also equipped with inverses for every element, what has changed?
options: It has stopped being associative.
It has become a group.
It has lost its identity element.
It has become only a binary operation, not a structure.

questions.question: Is the set of all invertible $2\times2$ matrices under multiplication a monoid?
options: No, because invertible matrices are not closed under multiplication.
No, because $I_2$ is not invertible.
Yes, with identity $I_2$.
Only if all matrices commute.

questions.question: Why is the phrase “with identity” not enough by itself to define a monoid?
options: The operation must be associative and binary on the set
An identity already makes the operation associative
The operation must also have inverses for every element
The operation must also be commutative on the set

questions.question: Why does a monoid support powers such as $a^0$ in a natural way?
options: The set must be a subset of real numbers
The identity element gives the empty product
The operation must be commutative.
Every element has an inverse.

questions.question: On positive real numbers with multiplication, which structure is present?
options: Not even a semigroup.
A monoid but not a group.
A semigroup but not a monoid.
A group, and therefore also a monoid.

questions.question: On all real numbers with multiplication, why is the structure a monoid but not a group?
options: The element $0$ has no multiplicative inverse.
Multiplication is not associative.
There is no multiplicative identity.
Real numbers are not closed under multiplication.
